title: Zeus looks away: the Battle at the Ships
greek: πάλιν τρέπεν ὄσσε φαεινώ (palin trepen osse phaeinō)
short: Sure that no god will interfere, Zeus turns his eyes from Troy; his lapse lets Poseidon start the long Greek recovery of Books 13-15.
body: Book 13 opens with a reversal. Zeus has brought Hector to the ships, and now he looks far away to the north, sure that no other god will dare to help either side. At once the narrator says that Poseidon 'kept no blind watch' (ἀλαοσκοπιή, an oxymoron, as Monro notes), and the sea-god uses the lapse. Ancient editors called this book 'The Battle at the Ships'. Leaf calls Books 13-15 'a great retardation': until Zeus wakes in Book 15, every Greek gain is matched by a Trojan one, so the crisis reached at the end of Book 12 is still unresolved at the end of Book 15. Monro finds Zeus's sudden indifference surprising. It also sits oddly with 13.345-60, where Zeus and Poseidon are pictured pulling against each other, and some critics have therefore doubted lines 1-9. Zeus's inattention here prepares for the more famous distraction in Book 14, when Hera puts him to sleep (Il. 14.153-353).

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1902), Introduction to Book XIII, pp. 1-2

title: Hippemolgi and Abii: the mare-milkers and the 'most righteous of men'
greek: Ἱππημολγοί γλακτοφάγοι, Ἄβιοι (Hippēmolgoi glaktophagoi, Abioi)
short: Peoples at the northern edge of the world: nomads who milk mares and drink milk, and the Abii, idealised as the justest of mankind.
body: Zeus's gaze passes over the Thracians and the Mysians, and Leaf and Monro both take these to be the European Mysians on the Danube, not the Asian Mysians of Il. 2.858. Then it reaches two half-legendary peoples. Hippemolgi means 'mare-milkers' and glaktophagoi 'milk-eaters'. Leaf and Monro identify them with the nomadic Scythians north of the Danube, whose diet of mares' milk Herodotus describes (4.2). Whether Abii is a name or an epithet was already disputed in antiquity. The LSJ lexicon gives the old rendering 'having no fixed subsistence', i.e. nomads, but prefers a proper name. Strabo argues the point at length (7.3.2-9). He defends Homer against Apollodorus, who claimed the poet had invented these peoples, and he cites Ephorus' praise of the just nomads. Leaf compares Herodotus' Argippaei, who settle their neighbours' disputes and carry no weapons (4.23), and the 'Gabioi' of Aeschylus' Prometheus Unbound, 'most just of mortals'. The line shows an early Greek habit of idealising remote peoples, as with the 'blameless Ethiopians' of Il. 1.423.

title: Samothrace, Poseidon's watch-tower
greek: Σάμος Θρηικίη (Samos Thrēikiē)
short: Homer's 'Thracian Samos': from its high peak Poseidon can see Ida, Troy and the ships; the Trojan plain really can see Samothrace over Imbros.
body: Homer says 'Thracian Samos'. The compound name Samothrace is later (Monro), and the island of Samos itself is never named in Homer. Strabo explains samos as an old word for 'heights' (Book 10, C 457, cited by Leaf). Leaf notes that the Trojan plain is in fact visible from the island's high central peak, over the top of Imbros. He calls this a rare mark of personal knowledge of the area, and suggests it points to a comparatively late passage. The traveller A. W. Kinglake records in Eothen (1844, ch. 4) that the map had made him doubt the line, because Imbros seemed to block the view. Then, standing in the Troad, he saw Samothrace towering beyond Imbros, 'the watch-tower of Neptune'. Monro calls this 'a well-known passage'. Later Samothrace was famous for the mysteries of the Great Gods (Herodotus 2.51), but Homer shows no knowledge of the cult.

title: Aegae and Poseidon's chariot over the sea
greek: Αἰγαί (Aigai)
short: Poseidon reaches his undersea palace at Aegae in four strides and drives his golden chariot over a rejoicing sea: a grand entrance for his intervention.
body: Poseidon crosses from Samothrace in four huge strides to Aegae, where his golden palace lies under the sea. There he yokes his bronze-hooved horses and drives over the waves. Sea-creatures play around him and the water parts 'in gladness', and he hobbles the horses with golden fetters in a cave between Tenedos and Imbros. Leaf notes that two places called Aegae, one in Achaea and one in Euboea, were both centres of Poseidon's cult (compare Il. 8.203). The old puzzle is that any Aegae lies farther from Samothrace than Troy does, so why should the god make the detour? Monro's answer is artistic: the god's intervention changes the course of the story, so it is marked by a set-piece entrance, much as an arming scene marks a hero's aristeia. Leaf finds the 'gorgeous but somewhat florid' imagery close in spirit to the Deception of Zeus. He also notes that crediting the sea with a human emotion is unique in Homer. Virgil models Neptune's sea-procession on this passage (Aen. 5.817-26), and Leaf notes an imitation in Moschus' Europa (115 ff.).

anchor: the Enfolder and Shaker of Earth
title: Enfolder and Shaker of Earth (Poseidon)
greek: γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος (gaiēochos ennosigaios)
short: Poseidon's paired titles: the earth-shaker, god of earthquakes, and gaiēochos, which may mean 'earth-holder' or 'earth-mover'.
body: Ennosigaios is straightforward: 'earth-shaker', from ἔνοσις (shaking) and γαῖα (earth). Poseidon is god of earthquakes as well as of the sea, and in the battle of the gods he makes Ida and Troy quake (Il. 20.57-60). Gaiēochos is disputed. The ancient derivation from ἔχω, 'hold', gave 'earth-holding' (Autenrieth), which suggests the sea embracing the land. Murray's 'Enfolder' follows that tradition. The LSJ lexicon instead derives the second element from the root of Latin veho, 'carry, move', and so renders 'earth-moving, earth-carrying'. It also records Γαιάοχος as the name of a contest at Sparta (IG V.1 296), and Pausanias saw a temple of Poseidon Gaiaochos near Therapne in Laconia (3.20.2). The title suits Book 13, which is Poseidon's book: he secretly organises the Greek resistance while Zeus looks away. In Iliad 15.187-93 he reminds Zeus that the three sons of Cronos divided the world by lot, and that the grey sea fell to him.

title: Recognising a god: Poseidon disguised as Calchas
greek: ἴχνια γὰρ μετόπισθε ποδῶν ἠδὲ κνημάων (ichnia gar metopisthe podōn ēde knēmaōn)
short: Gods enter battle in mortal disguise; Oilean Aias recognises Poseidon from behind, by the way his feet and legs move as he leaves.
body: Poseidon takes the form of the seer Calchas, strikes the two Aiantes with his staff to fill them with strength, and darts off like a hawk. Aias son of Oïleus realises that it was a god, because he recognised 'the ichnia of feet and legs' as the figure went away. 'Footprints' hardly fits 'legs', so the word was already debated in antiquity. Leaf prefers 'movements' (the gait), noting the ancient variant ἴχματα. Monro takes 'outlines', as though Poseidon began to resume his own shape as he left. Leaf compares Virgil's Venus, betrayed by her walk: 'vera incessu patuit dea' (Aen. 1.405). Gods are often recognised at the moment they leave, as when Athena departs as a bird (Od. 3.371-2). Poseidon will take another disguise at 13.216 (Thoas) and again at 14.136 (an old man).

title: 'The hearts of the noble can be healed'
greek: ἀκεσταί τοι φρένες ἐσθλῶν (akestai toi phrenes esthlōn)
short: Poseidon blames the rout on Agamemnon's quarrel with Akhilleus, then urges a quick cure: noble hearts can be mended.
body: Speaking as Calchas, Poseidon says the Trojans are at the ships 'because of the baseness of our leader'. The army, at odds with Agamemnon over his dishonouring of Akhilleus, will not fight. He then gives a maxim: ἀκεσταί, 'curable' (LSJ), are the hearts of the noble. What is to be healed? Leaf thinks the obvious reference is to the breach with Akhilleus. That reading is hard to square with Book 9, where Akhilleus has already refused amends, and Leaf takes the tension as a sign that the Embassy is late. Monro refers it instead to the soldiers' grudge against Agamemnon. Either way, the line sets the hope that noble tempers can be turned against the stubbornness of Akhilleus himself, whom Aias reproaches for an implacable heart (Il. 9.628-38). Compare Il. 15.203, 'the hearts of the noble can be turned'.

title: Aidōs and nemesis: shame and indignation
greek: αἰδῶ καὶ νέμεσιν (aidō kai nemesin)
short: The core of Homeric battle-ethics: aidōs, the shame one feels before others, and nemesis, the righteous indignation of others.
body: 'Set in your hearts, each of you, aidōs and nemesis.' Aidōs is a restraining sense of shame and respect, a sensitivity to how one looks in others' eyes. Nemesis is the indignation that wrongdoing arouses. LSJ calls aidōs 'subjective' and nemesis 'objective' here. Monro glosses them as sensitiveness to blame and a sense of wrong-doing, together 'such rudiments of moral sense' as Homer recognised. These are the standard words of battle exhortation: 'Αἰδώς, Argives!' (5.787), and 'feel aidōs before one another' (15.561-2). Hector, too, will not shirk battle because he feels aidōs before the Trojans (6.441-3). E. R. Dodds famously described Homeric society as a 'shame-culture'. Douglas Cairns's full-length study argues that aidōs is a subtler, internalised value than that label suggests.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books XIII-XXIV, with notes (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897), note on 13.121-122

title: The close formation round the Aiantes
greek: ἀσπὶς ἄρ' ἀσπίδ' ἔρειδε, κόρυς κόρυν, ἀνέρα δ' ἀνήρ (aspis ar' aspid' ereide, korus korun, anera d' anēr)
short: Shield on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man: a rare Homeric picture of a solid battle line, central to the debate about Homeric tactics.
body: The picked Greeks form a wall around the two Aiantes. Spear is fenced with spear and shield with overlapping shield, and the crests of their helmets touch whenever they nod. The rare word προθέλυμνος is puzzling. Monro takes it as 'overlapping', and compares the Roman testudo. Leaf suggests 'with base set forward', the stance of a warrior crouched behind a long shield. He notes that such close formation is rare in Homer and recurs at 12.105 and 16.212-17, and he thinks lines 131-3 were borrowed from Book 16. The passage is a key text in the long debate about Homeric warfare: was it a string of duels between champions, or mass fighting already close to the later hoplite phalanx? Joachim Latacz argued for pervasive mass combat. Hans van Wees describes a looser, more fluid order in which close formations like this one are occasional. The Spartan poet Tyrtaeus echoes the line to rouse hoplites: foot against foot, shield against shield, crest against crest (fr. 11.31-3 West).

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 13.130

anchor: like a boulder from a cliff
title: Hector as a rolling boulder
greek: ὀλοοίτροχος ὣς ἀπὸ πέτρης (oloöitrochos hōs apo petrēs)
short: Hector charges like a rock torn loose by a winter torrent: unstoppable until it reaches the level plain, where it stops 'for all its eagerness'.
body: Hector bounds down like a boulder that a winter flood has broken loose from a cliff-top. It leaps, the woods ring beneath it, and it runs on unchecked until it reaches the level plain, where it rolls no farther. The simile maps the narrative exactly: Hector threatens to break through to the sea, but he is halted when he meets the close-packed Greek ranks (13.145-8). Monro points out the Homeric pattern 'so long... but when', which here marks a movement and then its arrest. The rare word ὀλοοίτροχος occurs only here in Homer. Leaf derives it from the root 'roll' (Latin volvo), and Monro records Buttmann's alternative, 'destructive'. Murray's 'ruthless stone' renders ἀναιδής, literally 'shameless'. The same word describes Sisyphus' rolling stone in Od. 11.598. Leaf compares a similar simile in the Hesiodic Shield (437-42).

title: Mutilating the dead: Imbrius' head
greek: σφαιρηδὸν δ' ἑλιξάμενος (sphairēdon d' helixamenos)
short: In revenge for Amphimachus, Oilean Aias beheads the dead Imbrius and bowls the head through the crowd to Hector's feet.
body: Angry at the death of Amphimachus, Aias son of Oïleus cuts the head from Imbrius' corpse, swings round, and sends it rolling 'like a ball' through the throng until it lands in the dust before Hector. Leaf notes that this savage practice is rare in Homer, and compares Peneleos' trophy at 14.496-505 and Hector's wish to fix Patroclus' head on a stake (18.176-7). Monro adds that mutilating the dead was excused in Homer only as special revenge, while later Greeks thought it the mark of barbarians. In Herodotus, Pausanias refuses to mutilate the body of Mardonius for exactly that reason (9.79). Threats of outrage to corpses grow through the poem, from the dogs and birds of the proem to Akhilleus' treatment of Hector's body in Books 22-24. Charles Segal traced this as a structural theme of the Iliad.

title: Amphimachus, Poseidon's grandson
greek: υἱωνοῖο πεσόντος (huiōnoio pesontos)
short: Amphimachus, son of Cteatus, was Poseidon's grandson; his death turns the god's anger into active help for the Greeks.
body: Amphimachus was a leader of the Epeians (Il. 2.620-1). He was the son of Cteatus, one of the twin 'sons of Actor' whom Nestor fought in his youth. Nestor adds that their real father, Poseidon, saved them (11.709-10, 750-2). So the twins had a mortal father in name, Actor, and a divine one, Poseidon, a double paternity also recorded by Apollodorus (Library 2.7.2). Leaf calls the allusion 'unusually obscure', since Poseidon is not named in the lines where Amphimachus dies. Monro agrees that it is unlike Homer to leave this to be understood. Gods' care for their descendants is a recurring motive in these books: Ares will grieve for his son Ascalaphus (13.518-25, 15.110-42), and Zeus for Sarpedon in Book 16.

title: 'Even sorry men have valour when combined'
greek: συμφερτὴ δ' ἀρετὴ πέλει ἀνδρῶν καὶ μάλα λυγρῶν (sumphertē d' aretē pelei andrōn kai mala lugrōn)
short: Poseidon, disguised as Thoas, tells Idomeneus that united valour exists even among very poor fighters, and the two of them are better than that.
body: Literally: 'there is a combined valour even of very sorry men' (Leaf). LSJ glosses συμφερτός as 'united, in conjunction', and the word occurs only here in Homer. Monro paraphrases 'union makes prowess'. Leaf reports that Aristarchus already explained the line this way: valour can belong to a mass even when each member is weak. The gnome suits a book whose heroes fight in pairs and close formations: the Aiantes side by side like yoked oxen (13.701-8), Idomeneus with his squire Meriones, and the shield-wall of 13.126-35. Poseidon then caps the proverb: 'but we two know how to fight even with good men'. Compare Diomedes' 'when two go together, one sees before the other' (10.224-6).

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 13.237

title: The ambush (lochos) as the test of courage
greek: λόχος (lochos)
short: Idomeneus' portrait of fear: in an ambush the coward's colour changes and his teeth chatter, while the brave man stays steady.
body: Idomeneus tells Meriones that the true test of men is the ambush (λόχος, LSJ 'ambuscade'). There the coward betrays himself: his colour keeps changing, he cannot sit still but shifts from knee to knee, his heart pounds and his teeth chatter. The brave man's colour does not change, and he longs for the fighting to begin. Leaf explains χρώς as the complexion. Monro notes a play on λέγομαι, 'to be picked out' and 'to be recounted'. Waiting in silence for the enemy tests the nerve more than open battle. That is why Akhilleus taunts Agamemnon with never daring to go in ambush (1.226-7), and the wooden horse is itself called a lochos (Od. 4.277). Casey Dué and Mary Ebbott argue that ambush was a valued traditional theme of early Greek epic, an alternative to open warfare, not a debased one. They note that heroes such as Meriones belong to both kinds of fighting.

title: War as lovers' talk (oaristys)
greek: προμάχων ὀαριστύς (promachōn oaristus)
short: A word for the intimate talk of lovers is used for the front line of battle, an ironic metaphor that Homer uses again.
body: ὀαριστύς means 'familiar converse, fond discourse' (LSJ), the intimate talk of lovers. The same word names one of the charms in Aphrodite's love-band at 14.216. Applied to the front line it is an oxymoron (Leaf) and ironical (Monro). Compare 17.228, 'such is war's dalliance'. LSJ also allows a concrete sense here, 'the company of the front-fighters'. The figure is most moving at 22.126-8. There Hector, waiting for Akhilleus, knows that he cannot 'whisper' with him from an oak or a rock as a youth and a maiden whisper together. Homer often borrows the language of love and courtship for combat, and the language of war for love. Book 14 inverts the figure, when Hera arms herself for love.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 13.291

anchor: the Ephyri or the great-hearted Phlegyes
title: Ares and Rout among the Ephyri and Phlegyes
greek: Ἐφύρους ... Φλεγύας μεγαλήτορας; Φόβος (Ephurous ... Phleguas megalētoras; Phobos)
short: Idomeneus and Meriones go to war like Ares and his son Rout leaving Thrace to join one of two warring Thessalian tribes.
body: Idomeneus and Meriones march out like Ares and his son Phobos ('Rout', panic flight). The two arm in Thrace and go to join either the Ephyri or the Phlegyes, but grant glory to only one side. According to Strabo (Book 9, C 442, cited by Leaf and Monro), the Ephyri lived at Crannon in Thessaly and the Phlegyes at Gyrton. The Phlegyes were a legendary race of brigands. They attacked Thebes and Delphi and were destroyed by Apollo (Pausanias 9.36, cited by Leaf). Ares' home in Thrace recurs at Od. 8.361, and Virgil makes him lord of the Getic fields (Aen. 3.35). Hesiod makes Phobos and Deimos (Fear) children of Ares and Aphrodite (Theogony 933-6). Leaf finds the slide from simile into a description of Ares' habits somewhat harsh. The simile is double-edged: it exalts the Cretan pair, and it recalls that Ares favours only one side.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 13.299, 13.301

title: 'Eats the grain of Demeter': a formula for mortality
greek: ἔδοι Δημήτερος ἀκτήν (edoi Dēmētēros aktēn)
short: Mortals are bread-eaters: Aias will yield to no man who eats Demeter's grain and can be wounded by bronze or stones.
body: Idomeneus defines a mortal in three ways: one who eats the grain of Demeter, and who can be cut by bronze or crushed by stones. ἀκτή here is a poetic word for meal or ground corn. LSJ lists the phrase 'Demeter's grain' at 13.322 and 21.76, and Hesiod uses it for the threshed grain of the threshing-floor (Works and Days 597, 805). Eating bread marks humans off from gods. The gods 'eat no bread and drink no wine', and so they are bloodless and deathless (Il. 5.341-2). Mortals are 'those who eat the fruit of the field' (6.142). Demeter is barely a person here: her name stands for grain itself. The line sets Telamonian Aias at the outer limit of what a mortal can be, and the next lines yield only one superiority to Akhilleus, his speed of foot (13.324-5).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. ἀκτή (B)
G. Autenrieth, A Homeric Dictionary (trans. R. Keep, 1876), s.v. ἀκτή

title: Zeus the elder brother
greek: ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς πρότερος γεγόνει καὶ πλείονα ᾔδη (alla Zeus proteros gegonei kai pleiona ēidē)
short: Poseidon helps the Greeks only in secret because Zeus is the elder and wiser brother; Hesiod, by contrast, makes Zeus the youngest.
body: The narrator pauses to sum up the divine conflict. Zeus wants glory for Akhilleus and Thetis, but not the destruction of the Greeks. Poseidon, angry at the Greek defeat, helps them secretly 'in the likeness of a man', because Zeus 'was born first and knew more'. In the Iliad Zeus's seniority is the basis of his authority: he claims to be 'elder in birth' (15.166, 182). Hesiod tells the opposite story. Zeus is the youngest child of Cronos, saved from being swallowed when his elder brothers and sisters were not (Theogony 453-500). The Iliad also has the three brothers divide the world by lot (15.187-93). Leaf thinks lines 345-60 are a superfluous recapitulation, perhaps once the proem to this book or to the Deception of Zeus. Monro reads them as the poet pausing on the spectacle of the two sons of Cronos at odds.

anchor: knotted the ends of the cords
title: The rope of strife: the gods' tug-of-war
greek: ἔριδος κρατερῆς καὶ ὁμοιΐου πτολέμοιο πεῖραρ ἐπαλλάξαντες (eridos kraterēs ... peirar epallaxantes)
short: Zeus and Poseidon tie the armies to one unbreakable rope of war and pull it tight: a knot no one can loose, which looses many men's knees.
body: The two gods 'knotted the rope-end of mighty strife and evil war and drew it taut over both armies, a knot none might break or undo, that loosed the knees of many men'. Leaf follows Aristarchus' reading τώ ('the two', meaning the gods). He explains ἐπαλλάξαντες as crossing a rope over itself, so that the gods tie the armies to the rope and haul them back and forth. A variant reading made the armies themselves the teams in a tug-of-war. Monro shows the double sense of πεῖραρ: the literal 'end of a rope', and the abstract 'issue, limit', as in 'the ends of victory are held by the gods' (7.102). He also notes the grim play ἄλυτον ... λῦσε, 'unloosable... loosed'. The metaphor of strained war returns at 14.389-91, where Poseidon and Hector 'strain' the strife. The divine contest is paid for in mortal lives.

title: Othryoneus' suit for Cassandra: bride-price (hedna)
greek: ἀνάεδνον; ἕδνα (anaednon; hedna)
short: Othryoneus wooed Cassandra with a promised deed instead of bride-gifts; Idomeneus kills him and mocks the bargain.
body: Othryoneus of Cabesus, newly arrived 'following the rumour of war', asked Priam for Cassandra. He offered no ἕδνα (gifts from suitor to the bride's family, LSJ), only a promise to drive the Achaeans from Troy. Leaf compares David, who won Saul's daughter by killing Philistines instead of paying a dowry (1 Samuel 18:25). Idomeneus kills him and jeers that the Greeks would make the same promise and give him Agamemnon's fairest daughter, since they 'deal not hardly in exacting gifts of wooing'. Agamemnon had offered Akhilleus a daughter 'without bride-price' in all seriousness (9.146). In Homer Cassandra is simply the most beautiful of Priam's daughters, and the prophetess of later legend does not appear (Leaf). Homeric marriage gifts are inconsistent: bride-price paid to the father sits beside a dowry given with the bride. Anthony Snodgrass used this as evidence that the epic blends customs of different periods.

title: Hades the gate-keeper, and Deïphobus' boast
greek: εἰς Ἄϊδός περ ἰόντα πυλάρταο κρατεροῖο (eis Aïdos per ionta pulartao krateroio)
short: Hades is 'gate-fastener', who keeps the gates of the dead shut; Deïphobus jokes that the dead Asius now has an escort on the way.
body: πυλάρτης means 'gate-fastener' (LSJ, from ἀραρίσκω, 'fit, fasten'). Hades holds the gates of the underworld so that none return (Il. 8.367; Od. 11.277). Deïphobus' vaunt is a grim joke. Asius will go to Hades glad at heart, because Deïphobus has given him an 'escort' (πομπός), Hypsenor, as a host escorts a departing guest. Leaf calls the 'repeated taunts of the victors' a marked peculiarity of Book 13. The boasts form a chain: Idomeneus over Othryoneus (13.374-82), Idomeneus' 'three for one' (13.446-54), and Menelaus over Peisander (13.620-39). Leaf also notes a real difficulty. Deïphobus treats Hypsenor as dead, yet lines 420-3 have him carried off 'groaning heavily', a phrase used elsewhere of wounded men.

title: Alcathous spellbound, and the quivering spear
greek: θέλξας ὄσσε φαεινά, πέδησε δὲ φαίδιμα γυῖα (thelxas osse phaeina, pedēse de phaidima guia)
short: Poseidon bewitches the eyes and fetters the limbs of Alcathous, so he stands still for Idomeneus' spear; the dying heart shakes the spear-butt.
body: Alcathous, Anchises' son-in-law and 'the best man in wide Troy', is given a brief, tender biography. He married the eldest daughter of Anchises, who excelled all girls of her age in beauty, handiwork and wisdom, and he reared the young Aeneas. Poseidon 'enchanted' his eyes. θέλγω is the verb for magical bewitching (LSJ; Autenrieth glosses 'casts a blindness'). Alcathous stands fixed like a pillar or a leafy tree. Leaf compares Apollo stunning Patroclus (16.788-806). The spear lodges in his heart, and the still-beating heart makes its butt quiver until 'Ares stayed its fury'. Leaf thinks the image an exaggeration. Monro explains 'Ares' here as the spirit of war inhabiting the weapon, since the god himself sits on Olympus, unaware, at 13.521-5. Such short obituaries of minor warriors give each death its weight. The death also brings Aeneas into the fight.

title: Minos, Deucalion and the lineage of Idomeneus
greek: ὃς πρῶτον Μίνωα τέκε Κρήτῃ ἐπίουρον (hos prōton Minōa teke Krētēi epiouron)
short: Idomeneus boasts descent from Zeus: Zeus fathered Minos, 'warden of Crete', Minos fathered Deucalion, and Deucalion fathered Idomeneus.
body: Idomeneus answers Deïphobus' boast with his pedigree. ἐπίουρος means 'guardian, warden' (LSJ), and the same word is used of a chief swineherd at Od. 13.405. In the Odyssey Minos rules at Cnossus and is 'the familiar of great Zeus' (19.178-9), and he sits as judge among the dead (11.568-71). Zeus's love for 'the daughter of Phoenix', Europa in later tradition, who bore Minos and Rhadamanthys, is recalled at 14.321-2 (Leaf; Monro). This Deucalion is not the flood-hero, son of Prometheus. Genealogy is a weapon in Homeric vaunting: Aeneas and Glaucus also answer challenges with family history (20.200-58; 6.145-211). The modern name 'Minoan' for Bronze Age Cretan civilisation was taken from this mythical king.

title: Aeneas' grudge against Priam
greek: αἰεὶ γὰρ Πριάμῳ ἐπεμήνιε δίῳ (aiei gar Priamōi epemēnie diōi)
short: Aeneas hangs back because Priam never honoured him; a hint of rivalry between the two branches of the Trojan royal house.
body: Monro remarks that this quarrel is 'not elsewhere noticed'. Leaf links it to a tradition of rivalry between the houses of Anchises and Priam, perhaps reflecting a historical family in the Troad that claimed descent from Aeneas. In Book 20 Akhilleus taunts Aeneas with hoping to succeed Priam (20.178-83). Poseidon prophesies that Aeneas and his descendants will rule the Trojans (20.302-8), and Aphrodite makes the same promise to Anchises in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (196-7). Leaf also cites Menecrates of Xanthus, reported by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 1.48), for a story that Aeneas, slighted at Troy, betrayed the city. The verb ἐπεμήνιε contains μῆνις, the word for Akhilleus' wrath: like Akhilleus, Aeneas holds back because he has been denied honour (timē).

title: Ascalaphus, son of Ares, dies unknown to his father
greek: Ἀσκάλαφον ... υἱὸν Ἐνυαλίοιο (Askalaphon ... huion Enualioio)
short: Deïphobus kills Ares' son Ascalaphus, while Ares sits on Olympus under golden clouds, held back by Zeus and unaware.
body: Enyalius, 'the Warlike', is used in the Iliad both as an epithet of Ares and as his name (LSJ). Ascalaphus and his brother Ialmenus led the Minyans of Orchomenus, sons of Ares by Astyoche (2.511-16). The narrator stresses the god's ignorance: Ares sits on Olympus 'beneath the golden clouds', confined by Zeus's will with the other gods. Monro cites this as evidence that all the books from 11 onwards assume the gods are absent from the field. When Ares learns of the death, he arms to avenge his son in defiance of Zeus, and Athena has to restrain him (15.110-42). Even a god cannot save his son: the same pathos returns, on a larger scale, when Zeus lets Sarpedon die (16.431-61).

title: Zeus Xeinios and Menelaus' complaint
greek: Ζηνὸς ἐριβρεμέτεω χαλεπὴν ... μῆνιν ξεινίου (Zēnos eribremeteō chalepēn ... mēnin xeiniou)
short: Menelaus names the war's moral cause: Paris violated guest-friendship, protected by Zeus Xeinios, who will destroy Troy.
body: Standing over Peisander, Menelaus says the Trojans did not fear 'the grievous wrath of loud-thundering Zeus, god of guests' (ξείνιος, 'protector of strangers', Autenrieth). Paris carried off his wife and treasure after being entertained in his house. Leaf notes the emphasis given to Xeiniou by its position at the start of the line, as at Od. 9.271. This is the poem's clearest statement that the war is punishment for breaking xenia (compare Menelaus' prayer at 3.351-4). The speech then turns to bitter complaint against Zeus, who seems to favour the insolent. Men can have their fill of everything, of sleep, love, song and dance, but the Trojans are never sated with war. Leaf compares Pindar, Nemean 7.52-3, on satiety (κόρος) even of honey and love. Menelaus' list, sleep and love, looks forward to Book 14, where Zeus himself is overcome by both.

title: Harpalion's weeping father: a famous inconsistency
greek: μετὰ δέ σφι πατὴρ κίε δάκρυα λείβων (meta de sphi patēr kie dakrua leibōn)
short: Pylaemenes follows his son's body weeping, although Menelaus killed Pylaemenes in Book 5: a contradiction debated since antiquity.
body: Harpalion, son of the Paphlagonian king Pylaemenes, is shot by Meriones and dies 'like a worm'. His father walks weeping beside the chariot that carries the body. But Menelaus had killed Pylaemenes at 5.576-9. Leaf reports the ancient remedies. Aristophanes of Byzantium deleted lines 658-9. Aristarchus would either delete them or assume a second Pylaemenes. Zenodotus changed the name to 'Kylaimenes' at 643. Others said the father's ghost followed, or added a negative so that the father did not go. Leaf calls the contradiction 'glaring' but less important than many others. Monro thinks that in minor incidents the poet invented as needed, 'we are not to look for the exactness of a historian'. The episode is a classic test case for analysts, who saw in such slips the work of different poets, and for those who explain them as natural in long composition.

title: Poinē: blood-price
greek: ποινὴ δ' οὔ τις παιδὸς ἐγίγνετο τεθνηῶτος (poinē d' ou tis paidos egigneto tethnēōtos)
short: Poinē was compensation paid to a dead man's kin; to die with no blood-price or vengeance was a disgrace.
body: ποινή is 'blood-money, were-gild, fine paid by the slayer to the kinsmen of the slain' (LSJ). Ajax describes the custom when he rebukes Akhilleus: a man accepts compensation even for a murdered brother or son, and the killer may stay in the land (9.632-6). A dispute over the poinē for a slain man is one of the scenes on Akhilleus' shield (18.497-500). On the battlefield there is no payment, so poinē becomes vengeance, a life for a life. Acamas kills Promachus so that his brother's blood-price 'be not long unpaid' (14.483). Leaf notes that dying unavenged and uncompensated was a disgrace, comparing the outlaws of the Icelandic sagas. Harpalion's death is in fact avenged at once: his guest-friend Paris kills Euchenor.

title: Euchenor and the choice between two deaths
greek: Εὐχήνωρ; θωή (Euchēnōr; thōē)
short: Told he must die of illness at home or be killed at Troy, Euchenor chose Troy: a small-scale echo of Akhilleus' choice of two fates.
body: Euchenor, a rich and brave Corinthian, was the son of the seer Polyidus. His father had often told him he must either die of a painful disease at home or be killed by the Trojans at the ships. He sailed knowing this, and so escaped both the disease and the heavy fine (θωή, 'penalty', LSJ) that the Achaeans imposed on men who refused to serve. Leaf compares Echepolus of Sicyon, who gave Agamemnon a mare to avoid going to Troy (23.296-9). The story is a miniature of Akhilleus' two fates, a long life without glory or an early death with it (9.410-16), though Euchenor's motives are partly practical. Leaf notes that Pherecydes made Polyidus a descendant of the prophet Melampus. Paris shoots him beneath the ear in revenge for Harpalion.

title: The Ionians: their only appearance in Homer
greek: Ἰάονες ἑλκεχίτωνες (Iaones helkechitōnes)
short: The only mention of the Ionians in Homer, apparently meaning the Athenians; perhaps an Athenian addition to the text.
body: This is the only line in Homer where the Ionian name occurs (Leaf; Monro), and here the Ionians seem to be the Athenians led by Menestheus (689). Leaf suspects an Attic interpolation, meant to give ancient standing to Athens' later leadership of the Ionians. The epithet ἑλκεχίτωνες, 'with trailing tunics' (LSJ), recurs in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo (147), describing the Ionians gathered at Delos, and Thucydides quotes those lines (3.104). Monro, following Helbig, explains the long chiton as a mark of age, rank or festival dress. The whole list of contingents in 685-700, with the Phthians named only here, is unlike Homer's usual practice according to both Leaf and Monro. The Ionians of Asia Minor were, by most ancient accounts, the people among whom Homeric epic took shape.

title: Exile for homicide: Medon
greek: ἄνδρα κατακτάς, γνωτὸν μητρυιῆς Ἐριώπιδος (andra kataktas, gnōton mētruiēs Eriōpidos)
short: Medon, Oïleus' bastard son, lived far from home because he had killed a kinsman of his stepmother; exile was the usual answer to homicide.
body: Medon, bastard son of Oïleus and half-brother of the lesser Aias, lived in Phylace 'far from his native land'. He had killed a relative of his stepmother Eriopis. Leaf notes that γνωτός can mean brother or, more loosely, kinsman. In the Homeric world a killer who could not settle with the dead man's family by blood-price fled abroad, and often found a new place of honour there. Patroclus came to Peleus after killing a boy over a game of dice (23.85-90). Tlepolemus fled after killing his father's uncle (2.661-7), and Lycophron joined Aias after a killing (15.430-2). Medon himself commands Philoctetes' men in the Catalogue (2.726-8). Leaf points out that 694-7 are repeated at 15.333-6, where Aeneas kills Medon and the lines fit more naturally. Michael Gagarin's study of early Greek homicide law starts from such Homeric scenes.

anchor: trusting in bows and well-twisted slings
title: The Locrian archers and slingers
greek: τόξοισιν καὶ ἐϋστρεφεῖ οἰὸς ἀώτῳ (toxoisin kai eustrephei oios aōtōi)
short: The Locrians have no helmets, shields or spears; they shoot from behind with bows and wool slings, a rare glimpse of light-armed troops.
body: The Locrians do not follow Oilean Aias into close combat, because they have no bronze helmets, round shields or ash spears. They came to Troy trusting in bows and slings of twisted sheep's wool, and from behind the armoured front rank their volleys confuse the Trojans. In the Catalogue their leader Aias is small and wears a linen corselet (2.527-35). Leaf explains that the fully armed chief does not fight among his light-armed men, and he judges the decisive effect of the archers 'not epic'. Monro finds it strange that the Greeks cannot repel Hector at 687, yet the Trojans are almost routed by archers at 723. Light-armed fighters are usually anonymous in the Iliad, and archery carries some stigma: Diomedes sneers at Paris as a 'bowman' (11.385-95).

anchor: To one man hath God given
title: Polydamas, Hector's prudent counsellor
greek: ἄλλῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα (allōi men gar edōke theos polemēia erga)
short: Polydamas tells Hector that the gods give different gifts, war to one and good counsel to another; Hector listens now but not later.
body: Polydamas calls Hector 'hard to persuade' (ἀμήχανος, Leaf: 'intractable') and reminds him that the god gives works of war to one man, dance and song to another, and a wise mind to a third. He advises regrouping, and fears 'a man insatiate of war' still waiting at the ships, Akhilleus. This is one of several warnings he gives (12.60-79, 12.210-29, 18.249-83). The poem later says that the two men were born on the same night, one better with words and the other with the spear (18.251-2). Hector accepts the advice here but rejects it fatally in Book 18, and regrets it before his death (22.99-103). Monro calls Polydamas the 'cautious adviser' and, like Leaf, finds this scene loosely handled. Compare the same gnome on the uneven distribution of gifts in Odysseus' speech at Od. 8.167-77.

title: Hector 'like a snowy mountain'
greek: ὄρεϊ νιφόεντι ἐοικώς (oreï niphoenti eoikōs)
short: A puzzling simile: Hector rushing through the battle is compared to a snow-covered mountain; scholars disagree about its point.
body: Hector sets off 'like a snowy mountain', shouting as he goes. Monro calls the comparison 'a violent hyperbole' and especially unsuited to a man described as moving fast. Leaf rejects Nitzsch's idea that ὄρεϊ νιφόεντι means an avalanche. He argues that the words cannot bear that sense and that avalanches would hardly have been familiar to poets on the Aegean coasts, and he thinks attempts to emend the text are futile. Some readers take the point to be towering size and brilliance rather than motion, perhaps a gleaming helmet and crest. Virgil seems to have read it that way. When Aeneas turns to face Turnus, he is as great as Athos, Eryx or father Appenninus 'raising his snowy head to the sky' (Aen. 12.701-3), a simile Leaf cites as the imitation of this one.

title: 'Lily-like skin': Hector's sneer at Aias
greek: χρόα λειριόεντα (chroa leirioenta)
short: Hector mockingly calls the massive Aias' flesh 'lily-like', delicate and tender, before threatening it with his spear and the dogs.
body: λειριόεις, 'lily-like', occurs in Homer only in a transferred sense (LSJ). It is used of the 'lily voice' of the old men on the wall, compared to cicadas (3.152), and in Hesiod of the Muses' voice (Theogony 41). Applied to skin it suggests something delicate, soft or pale, and Leaf reads it here as ironic: 'that fair tender flesh'. The insult is pointed because Aias is the largest Greek warrior, famous for his tower-like shield (7.219-23). Hector's threat that Aias will glut the dogs and birds of Troy recalls the proem (1.4-5). An eagle has just appeared on the right, a good omen for the Greeks, and Hector brushes it aside, as he did Polydamas' bird-sign at 12.231-43. The book ends with both armies' shout reaching 'the aether and the splendour of Zeus'.
